claim: Profile-gated shared-memory chain scorer: 5.58x speedup on a chain-hot fixture, with the small-input control unchanged within 1.3% at the median.
kind: single-system ablation (xlog against its own baseline)

hardware.device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 3000 Blackwell Generation Laptop GPU
hardware.device_provenance: the measurement bundle itself does not record the device; it is attributed from the same campaign's runtime probe (docs/evidence/2026-05-18-v080-exact/runtime_probe.json, one day earlier, same host paths and same kernel packaging)

code_version.measurement_commit_subject: feat(v086): add chain exact shared-memory scorer

how_to_reproduce.ab_method: the same fixture is run twice in one process, once with the shared-memory path enabled and once disabled

small_control.role: below the gate threshold (baseline scorer must run unchanged)

protocol.dispersion_note: min and max seconds are recorded per arm; per-iteration times were not emitted, so the range is min-max rather than an IQR

small_control.delta_sign_note: regression_percent is computed by the runner as (smem_median - baseline_median) / baseline_median * 100, so the recorded -1.3218% means the shared-memory arm's median is 1.32% FASTER than the baseline's: the small-input control does not regress, and the 5% small-case guard is met with room. The min-max ranges of the two arms overlap, so the paper reports the control as unchanged within 1.3% rather than claiming a gain. The earlier draft of the paper described this figure as a 1.3% regression, which inverted the sign.

caveats: Point medians on two synthetic fixtures; no per-fixture dispersion beyond min-max was collected.

No committed test executes the shared-memory kernel: the exact-induction parity tests use fixtures below the gate threshold and therefore exercise only the baseline scorer. Parity above the threshold is established by this A/B run, not by the test suite.
Parity is compared on the public coverage signature, which is identical across the two arms on both fixtures.
